speaker: Astro Teller
en: Well, I mean, I was a serial tech entrepreneur before I became the co-founder and now the leader of X. The Moonshot Factory here at Alphabet. Before that, I did a PhD in artificial intelligence a long time ago. So I'm slightly academic. I'm a dyed in the wool entrepreneur. So I'm not sure I would describe myself as a nurturer of moonshots and moonshot takers. I'll start here, taking moonshots is really easy, super easy. If you don't care about efficiency, you find really high energy people who think they're right and are pretty smart. You dump a bunch of money on them and you'll get some moonshots, or anyway, some fairly big companies anyway. It's just not an efficient process and so, what I was somewhat interested in almost since I was a kid but which I've become obsessed with over the last twenty years, is how do you systematize radical innovation? And so what the Moonshot Factory is, is an attempt to explore these over the horizon sort of radical innovation things. That if they turned out to be as good as they seem on the surface, you could turn them into enduring businesses that are really good for the world. But shooting for that kind of thing, mostly the answer is nope, not now, can't be done at all, you can do it but you can't do it profitably, the world doesn't want it, whatever that is. So how do you figure out the one or two percent of the things that you start, that will be once in a generation opportunities for the world and for your investor? zh: 嗯,我是说,在我成为 X——Alphabet 旗下的登月工厂——的联合创始人以及现在的负责人之前,我是一个连续科技创业者。在那之前,很久以前我读过人工智能方向的博士。所以我有点学术背景。我是一个彻头彻尾的创业者。过去十六年,作为登月项目的船长,在 Alphabet 的登月工厂,我做了相当多的事情。所以我不确定我会把自己描述为登月项目的培育者和登月项目的尝试者。我先从这里说起,尝试登月项目真的很容易,超级容易。如果你不在乎效率,你找那些精力旺盛、自认为正确而且相当聪明的人。你往他们身上砸一大笔钱,你就会得到一些登月项目,或者无论如何,一些相当大的公司。只是这个过程并不高效,而我从差不多小时候起就有点感兴趣、但在过去二十年里变得痴迷的事情,是如何把颠覆性创新系统化?所以登月工厂就是一个尝试,去探索这些地平线之外的颠覆性创新的东西。如果它们最终证明和表面看起来一样好,你就可以把它们变成对世界真正有益的持久业务。但瞄准那种东西,大部分时候答案都是:不,现在不行,根本做不到,你能做但不赚钱,世界不想要它,诸如此类。那么你怎么搞清楚你启动的事情里那百分之一到百分之二,将成为对世界和对你的投资人来说千载难逢的机会?在这个案例里,Alphabet 是我们的投资人,以及如何尽可能高效地做到这一点。这就是登月工厂真正的由来。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: And I think that's the key difference that I was pointing out. Which is most of these classical founders, they have one idea, one moonshot, and they're kind of all in on that thing. And that's the thing they're going to do. Maybe they pivot once or twice, but that's really the company. How it's all set up, maybe a little bit of the origin story, just to get us enough of an understanding of the situation and then we're going to go deep on the process that you were just alluding to.
zh: 我想这就是我指出的关键区别。也就是大多数这些经典的创始人,他们有一个想法,一个登月项目,他们基本上全都押在那个东西上。那就是他们要做的事情。也许他们转向一两次,但那真的就是这家公司。你的设置在设计上就是不同的,你们在不断想出新的登月项目,尝试它们,测试它们,它是一个创造这些产出的系统。也许再多讲一点登月工厂的设置。它是如何搭建起来的,也许讲一点起源故事,好让我们对情况有足够的了解,然后我们再深入你刚才暗示的那个流程。

speaker: Astro Teller
en: Sure, so we were set up 16 years ago and we were set up because Google at the time was already starting to imagine Alphabet. Though Alphabet hadn't been named and so the desire was for there to be a kind of 21st century Bell Labs. That would park itself next to Google, not solve Google's problems. There are a lot of smart people at Google solving Google's problems. But to go find really new problems for this thing, which ended up being called Alphabet, the parent company of Google. To have, and then hopefully to solve some of those problems. Now, out of this process sometimes we come up with something. Google Brain is the most famous example, where we started and then it turns out to be so important to Google that we move it back to Google. And of course we can be proud of doing that. It's not an independent business, but it's been profoundly important for Alphabet, for the world. Sometimes we make something and we set it up as a separate business inside of Alphabet. Many of your listeners will know about Waymo, the self-driving cars, they came from X, or Wing, the drones for package delivery. That came from X, and so we have set up a number of businesses. Which are these sort of independent entities, but that are still inside the Alphabet umbrella and then increasingly frequently, when it makes sense, we create one of these moonshots when it's ready to graduate from X as an independent business. If Alphabet owns forty nine percent of that thing and doesn't have a board seat, then they're off to the races. We can cheer for them. They're still able to be very strategically involved with Alphabet, but they're in a really independent company at that point and so our job is to try one thousand, maybe fifteen hundred ideas per decade.
zh: 好的,我们是十六年前成立的,成立的原因是谷歌在当时已经开始设想 Alphabet。虽然 Alphabet 还没有被命名,所以愿望是有一个类似二十一世纪贝尔实验室的东西。它会把自己安置在谷歌旁边,不去解决谷歌的问题。谷歌有很多聪明人在解决谷歌的问题。而是去为这个后来被叫做 Alphabet 的东西、谷歌的母公司,寻找真正新的问题。去拥有,然后希望能解决其中一些问题。现在,在这个过程中,有时我们会做出点什么。Google Brain 是最著名的例子,我们启动了它,然后发现它对谷歌太重要了,于是我们把它移回谷歌。当然我们可以为此感到自豪。它不是一个独立业务,但它对 Alphabet、对世界都极其重要。有时我们做出一个东西,把它设为 Alphabet 内部的一个独立业务。你们的很多听众会知道 Waymo,自动驾驶汽车,它们来自 X,还有 Wing,送货无人机。那个也来自 X,所以我们设立了若干业务。这些是某种独立实体,但仍在 Alphabet 的大伞之内,然后越来越频繁地,在合理的时候,我们创造的某个登月项目到了可以从 X 毕业成为独立业务的时候。如果 Alphabet 拥有那个东西百分之四十九的股份,并且没有董事会席位,那它们就可以大展宏图了。我们可以为它们欢呼。它们仍然能够与 Alphabet 保持非常紧密的战略联系,但在那时它们已经是一家真正独立的公司了,所以我们的任务是每十年尝试一千个,也许一千五百个想法。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Completely agree and any of those businesses, Google Brain, Waymo. I mean, these are businesses that are once in a generation type businesses. Just about any founder that I know would be more excited to have one of those, let alone multiple of them. speaker: Astro Teller
en: But pretend that we were in this dialogue. You're a founder and you're thinking of coming to X, but you kind of want to know, what am I signing up for here? So one of the fundamental things I would want you to know is, if you have something you just really believe in, please do not come to X. I would analogize that, I know this doesn't sound super friendly. If you want to go to Vegas and you just believe that seventeen is your lucky number, and you want to bet on seventeen on the roulette wheel. Okay, more power to you, I guess, and it might come up seventeen. And you'll make a lot of money. So I'm not saying no, I'm just, but I'm telling you for sure, that's not what happens at X. At X, we're trying to be the card counters of innovation. So it is a very different process. If you come to X, I want you to work on making a moonshot. But I also want you to understand you will be wrong over and over and over again. What I owe you, what all of X owes you, if you're going to join us, is that we have to be serious about not punishing you when you're wrong. That as long as you're pursuing potential moonshots in really smart, scrappy ways and being intellectually honest about how it's going. If the answer is nope, this is not pulling our average up, let's just put a bullet in its head and move on. Bad news, you get no equity while you're here at X. But the good news is you haven't bet your kid's college fund on the teleporter. So if the teleporter turns out not to be the right thing for us to do, and we're actually going to celebrate you for stopping it. Because you're being intellectually honest, you just get to try again and maybe the time machine will work out if that's the next project that you try. So if it appeals to you to be more of a card counter, to be part of a process with zero friction and high flow. Where we're collectively exploring which of the things that we're currently looking at might be a Waymo, might be a Google Brain. If that excites you, come here and do it and the amazing news is at the end of, you might try several, they fail. Finally you try one and it actually gets all the way through X. You graduate, we give that team founders shares. A lot of the company goes to them, and you took no risk the whole time while you were doing it. And we can afford to do that because we're so much more efficient at stopping the things that aren't really great pretty early in the process. So it is a very different way of being an entrepreneur but for at least a class of entrepreneurs, typically ones who've already been to the wars once or twice.
zh: 但假装我们正在进行这场对话。你是一个创始人,正在考虑来 X,但你有点想知道,我在这里要承担的是什么?所以我想让你知道的一个根本性的事情是,如果你有一个你就是深信不疑的东西,请不要来 X。我会这样类比,我知道这听起来不太友好。如果你想去拉斯维加斯,你就是相信十七是你的幸运数字,你想在轮盘上押十七。行,祝你好运吧,我猜,也许真的会开出十七。而你会赚很多钱。所以我不是说不,我只是,但我确定地告诉你,那不是 X 发生的事情。在 X,我们努力成为创新的算牌者。所以这是一个非常不同的流程。如果你来 X,我希望你致力于做出一个登月项目。但我也希望你明白,你会一次又一次又一次地犯错。我欠你的,整个 X 欠你的,如果你要加入我们,就是我们必须认真地做到:当你错的时候不惩罚你。只要你以非常聪明、非常精干的方式追求潜在的登月项目,并且对进展保持智识上的诚实。如果答案是不,这没有拉高我们的平均水平,我们就干脆给它一枪然后继续前进。坏消息是,你在 X 期间没有股权。但好消息是你没有把孩子的大学基金押在传送机上。所以如果传送机最后证明不是我们该做的事,我们实际上会为叫停它而庆祝你。因为你在保持智识上的诚实,你只需要再试一次,也许时间机器会成功,如果那是你下一个尝试的项目。所以如果当个算牌者更吸引你,成为零摩擦、高心流的流程的一部分。我们在共同探索我们正在看的这些东西中哪一个可能是 Waymo,可能是 Google Brain。如果这让你兴奋,来这里做吧,而最棒的消息是,到最后,你可能试了好几个,它们都失败了。最后你试了一个,它真的走完了 X 的全程。你毕业了,我们给那个团队创始人股份。公司很大一部分归他们,而你在整个过程中没有承担任何风险。我们能负担得起这一点,是因为我们在流程早期就停掉那些其实不伟大的东西这件事上高效得多。所以这是一种非常不同的创业者方式,但对至少一类创业者来说,通常是那些已经上过一两次战场的人。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: They know how hard it is, that's right.

speaker: Astro Teller
en: Oh yeah, they're like, I know how hard it is and I know how much luck is involved. And I know the reality distortion field, like I'm sick of that. I want to be part of a team that's much more sort of intellectually, honestly trying to churn through ideas as thoughtfully, as efficiently as possible.
zh: 哦对,他们就像,我知道有多难,我也知道运气占多大成分。我也知道现实扭曲力场,我受够了那个。我想成为一个团队的一员,这个团队在尽可能深思熟虑、尽可能高效地流转各种想法上,更智识诚实一些。

speaker: Astro Teller
en: So at the very early part of the process, we look at one to two hundred ideas per year in enough detail that they get a code name. In the very early part of the process, no person is full time on any one of those projects. At the very least, we would ask you to have a major and a minor. Because the chances of the thing that you have a major on, that you're spending at least half of your time on, stopping in the next six months is very high. You need to not feel existentially tied. You have to not worry too much about your job and you have to worry less about what people will think of you, or what you think of yourself. If the thing you're currently working on turns out not to be the right answer, since most of them are not the right answer.
zh: 所以在流程非常早期的阶段,我们每年会以足够的深度审视一到两百个想法,让它们获得一个代号。在流程非常早期的阶段,没有任何一个人全职投入其中任何一个项目。至少,我们会要求你有一个主修和一个辅修。因为你主修的那个东西、你至少花一半时间在上面的那个东西,在未来六个月内停止的概率非常高。你需要感觉不到生存层面的绑定。你不必太担心你的工作,你也不必太担心别人怎么看你,或者你怎么看你自己,万一你正在做的那个东西最后证明不是正确答案,因为它们大多数都不是正确答案。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: And am I right in thinking that that's less about the cost per idea? Like, one person doing two things costs you less than one person doing one. and more about the psychology of it?
zh: 我这样理解对吗,这不主要是关于每个想法的成本?比如,一个人做两件事比一个人做一件事成本更低。而更多是关于心理层面?

speaker: Astro Teller
en: It's entirely about the psychology, because we'll often have two or three people part time on each idea. So we could just have one person a hundred percent on the idea. But first of all, people are smarter together in groups than they are individually. It's easier to be dispassionate and to be honest with yourself when there's other people who are poking at the thing with you. That means you can go and get a world expert in electrochemistry, a world expert in 3D printing, who we have on staff, for the five or ten percent of their time that you need without actually having to hire anybody. Because they're all part of X. So you get to actually act like a ten or fifteen person company with nobody actually feeling too existentially tied to it. So again, if you were coming to X, I would want you to really watch the following. You're going to need to move your sense of self worth from winning, which is what you, me, all of us were trained since we were five years old. I am good if I win. I'm good if I get an A plus on the test. That is not how X works. You will be miserable at X if you tie your sense of self worth to that. You have to rewire your sense of self worth to how wisely you can explore ideas and how viciously. In fact, we can attack our own ideas and pressure test them to see which ones survive.
zh: 这完全关乎心理,因为我们常常会有两三个人兼职投入每个想法。我们本可以让一个人百分之百投入一个想法。但首先,人们在一起、在群体里比 individually 更聪明。当有其他人和你一起戳那个东西时,更容易保持冷静、对自己诚实。这意味着你可以去请一位电化学领域的世界专家、一位 3D 打印领域的世界专家——我们团队里有这样的人——用你需要的那百分之五到百分之十的时间,而不必真的雇任何人。因为他们都是 X 的一部分。所以你实际上可以表现得像一家十到十五人的公司,而没有人感觉自己生存层面被绑死。所以再说一次,如果你来 X,我会希望你特别注意以下几点。你需要把你的自我价值感从赢得比赛上移开,而那是你、我、我们所有人从五岁起就被训练成的。我赢了我就好。我考试拿 A 加我就好。X 不是那样运作的。如果你把自我价值感绑定在那个上面,你在 X 会很痛苦。你必须把你的自我价值感重连到你探索想法有多智慧,以及我们能多狠地——事实上,我们就是可以——攻击自己的想法并给它们做压力测试,看哪些能存活下来。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Are there people that have been at X for five years, ten years, and never had any idea become a big success?
zh: 有没有人在 X 待了五年、十年,却从来没有一个想法变成大成功?

speaker: Astro Teller
en: Yeah, there are lots of people who are very good at beating up on ideas or helping to rapid prototype the ideas. So they're awesome Xers, but they never started an idea. By the way, another thing that's easy to say but very hard to rewire around is we literally don't track whose idea it was. We don't let people talk about who founded the idea.
zh: 是的,有很多人非常擅长打击想法,或者帮助快速原型化想法。所以他们是很棒的 Xer,但他们从没启动过一个想法。顺便说一句,另一件说来容易但 rewiring 起来非常难的事是,我们真的不去追踪那个想法是谁的。我们不允许人们谈论是谁创始了这个想法。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Interesting.
zh: 有意思。

speaker: Astro Teller
en: Because the ideas are easy. Ideas are trivially easy. We have a thousand ideas a year, that many of them just don't even get code names. Ideas are not the hard part. Our alpha comes from how efficiently we can discover which ideas are valuable. So if you want to be a cool Xer, if you want to have street cred here. It's not because you came up with the idea. Who cares? It's because you helped us kill the idea or figure out this sort of perspective shift that takes an idea from good to great.
zh: 因为想法是容易的。想法是显而易见地容易。我们每年有一千个想法,其中很多甚至拿不到代号。想法不是难的部分。我们的 alpha 来自我们能多高效地发现哪些想法有价值。所以如果你想当一个酷酷的 Xer,如果你想在这里有 street cred。不是因为你想出了那个点子。谁在乎?而是因为你帮我们杀掉了那个想法,或者想出了那种让想法从好变到伟大的视角转换。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: So before we get into that, I do want to touch a little bit on. As much as you say it's easy. Where do those, you said two hundred ideas per year that actually get a code name, which means there's probably more before that that don't, but where do those come from? How are you sourcing those ideas?
zh: 那在我们深入之前,我确实想稍微聊一下。尽管你说它很容易。那些——你说的每年两百个真正拿到代号的——想法,意味着在那之前可能还有更多拿不到的,它们从哪来?你们是怎么 sourcing 这些想法的?

speaker: Astro Teller
en: So sometimes they come from Xers. They almost never come from me. I do that on purpose because I don't want this to be the Astro show. A lot of places get over controlled by the people at the top, not just controlled in the hierarchy sense, but controlled in the sort of mental and creativity sense. I want this to be a very bottoms up place.
zh: 有时它们来自 Xer。它们几乎从不来自我。我是故意这样做的,因为我不想让这变成 Astro 秀。很多地方被顶层的人过度控制,不只是层级意义上的控制,而是心理和创造力意义上的控制。我想让这是一个非常自下而上的地方。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Is it also the danger of people saying, oh, Astro likes this idea. So let's invest more in this one because it's going to go further?
zh: 是不是也有这样的危险:人们会说,哦,Astro 喜欢这个想法。所以我们多投这个,因为它会走得更远?

speaker: Astro Teller
en: Yeah, so I don't let us play that game. I'm a truth seeker. I'm like, oh you're working on the teleporter. It's not like I don't want the teleporter to win. But if the teleporter is not going to be a Waymo, I want to know now. I don't want to know in three years, and I want you to be with me in wanting to know now, and not wanting to know in three years. So I don't want you to work on the stuff that's like, live to fight another day.
zh: 是的,所以我不让我们玩那个游戏。我是一个真理追寻者。我会说,哦,你在做传送机。我不是不希望传送机赢。但如果传送机不会成为 Waymo,我现在就想知道。我不想三年后才知道,而且我想让你和我一起,想现在知道,而不是想三年后知道。所以我不想让你做那种,活下来改日再战的事情。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Right.
zh: 对。

speaker: Astro Teller
en: Live to fight another day is absolutely what happens in the rest of Silicon Valley. But every entrepreneur knows in their hearts that that's actually like building a ladder to the moon. All these band-aids, they hate it, they all hate it. So let's work on the thing that really teaches us, is this going to change the world or not? I don't care if anyone pays for it right now, let's answer the scariest questions. When the scariest question left is, will someone pay for it? Then we better go get someone to pay for it.
zh: 活下来改日再战,这正是硅谷其他地方绝对会发生的事情。但每个创业者在心里都知道那其实就像造一架通往月球的梯子。所有这些创可贴,他们讨厌它,他们都讨厌它。所以我们来做真正能教会我们的事情:这会不会改变世界?我不在乎现在有没有人为它付钱,我们来回答最吓人的问题。当剩下最吓人的问题是,会有人为它付钱吗?那我们最好去找个人来付钱。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: We talk about this in the context of the podcast as, before startup mode there's research mode and having interviewed a lot of founders. Not all of them are good at this phase of figuring out if it's even the right idea to go after. A lot of founders have the DNA of being sellers or builders, so they want to get going, they want to get started, and they just want to start punching through walls, and making things happen. As you say, build that ladder to the moon. Whatever it is, just make it become reality without taking that first step that's a little bit more detached. Where you're able to very easily dismiss something, let something go to move to the next one and the problem becomes you might spend three years or five years on an idea. That is literally you pushing a boulder up a hill and it's just never going to get easy on the other side.
zh: 我们在播客的语境里聊过这个,叫做在 startup 模式之前有 research 模式,我采访过很多创始人。并非所有的人都擅长这个阶段,即搞清楚这是不是值得追的正确想法。很多创始人有销售者或建造者的 DNA,所以他们想动起来,想开始,他们只想开始凿穿墙壁,把事情推动起来。就像你说的,造那架通往月球的梯子。不管是什么,就是要让它变成现实,而不走第一步、那个更抽离一点的步骤。在那个步骤里,你能够非常轻易地否掉一个东西,放下一个东西去转到下一个,而问题是你可能会在一个想法上花三年或五年。那真的是你在把一块巨石推上山,而在山另一边永远不会变轻松。

speaker: Astro Teller
en: I would say the vast majority are doing that to some extent. Now, you can make that less likely as an entrepreneur if you make sure that you can see your goal from where you are. If you can see your goal, metaphorically speaking. Where the only really hard thing is how fast you run getting from here to there. That's what startups are built for and that's totally not what X is built for. But if your goal is over the horizon, you don't even know what direction it is and it might not even exist. So I think of it like, if we were lost in a rowboat. Somehow people get in this mindset of how vigorously I row is going to save us. You know what? If we're lost in a rowboat, I'm going to spend ninety percent of my time with the sextant and ten percent of my time rowing. But that is a really hard thing to get people to unlearn because they have learned that progress is the ultimate metric instead of learning being the ultimate metric. But especially while we're at X, because we're not yet company building. We do things that look more and more like company building. But we're buying options on the future and so information gain, the learning per dollar, is what we're actually trying to maximize. Now over time, of course, we do have to start answering questions like, does anyone want this thing? How much would it cost for us to make this thing? How much would people pay for this thing? Is the second number larger than the first? Ultimately you have to ask and answer questions that start sounding like business questions, but we do it as a set of experiments. We still even there say, we're not trying to find something people will buy and then sell a lot of it. We're trying to deeply understand, is there a dent in the universe to be made here? And if so, what's the right way to do it? The ideas come from all over the world. We often will find in a university, someone has some cool thing. I don't know, at Johns Hopkins, someone invented a frictionless surface. A frictionless surface is not a moonshot. That is a raw technology opportunity. Someone else might be really interested in ending warfare. Ending warfare sounds like a nice thing to do. Humanity is not better for wars, but that's also not a moonshot. The trick is to find a bunch of needs and technology pieces, and mush them together in a really surprising way. So we're not the paradigm shifting scientists. That's not what we do. We're paradigm shifting system engineers. We're trying to bridge that gap between basic science and something that's like venture investable. But that's like often a five or six year gap that gets filled very badly.
zh: 我会说绝大多数人在某种程度上都在那样做。现在,作为创业者,你可以让这种情况更不容易发生,如果你确保你能从你所在的位置看到你的目标。如果你能看到你的目标,打个比方。唯一真正难的事情是你从这儿跑到那儿有多快。那是 startup 为之而生的,而那完全不是 X 为之而生的。但如果你的目标在地平线之外,你甚至不知道它是什么方向,而且它可能根本不存在。所以我是这么想的,如果我们迷失在一艘划艇上。不知怎么地,人们会陷入一种心态,觉得我划得多卖力就能救我们。你知道吗?如果我们迷失在一艘划艇上,我会把百分之九十的时间花在六分仪上,百分之十的时间用来划桨。但让人们 unlearn 这一点真的很难,因为他们学到的是进展是终极指标,而不是学习是终极指标。但尤其当我们在 X 的时候,因为我们还不是在造公司。我们做的事情看起来越来越像造公司。但我们在购买未来的期权,所以信息增益,每一美元换来的学习,才是我们真正想最大化的。当然,随着时间推移,我们确实必须开始回答这样的问题:有人想要这个东西吗?造这个东西要花多少钱?人们会为这个东西付多少钱?第二个数字比第一个大吗?最终你必须提出并回答那些听起来像商业问题的东西,但我们把它作为一组实验来做。我们甚至在那里仍然会说,我们不是在找人们会买的东西然后卖掉很多。我们是在努力深入理解,这里有没有一个可以在宇宙上留下的凹痕?如果有,正确的方式是什么?这些想法来自世界各地。我们经常会在一所大学里发现,有人做出了某个很酷的东西。我不知道,在约翰霍普金斯,有人发明了一个无摩擦表面。无摩擦表面不是一个登月项目。那是一个原始的技术机会。另一个人可能真的对终结战争感兴趣。终结战争听起来是件好事。战争不会让人类更好,但那也不是一个登月项目。诀窍在于找到一堆需求和技术碎片,以一个真正令人惊讶的方式把它们糅合在一起。所以我们不是范式转换的科学家。那不是我们做的。我们是范式转换的系统工程师。我们试图跨越基础科学和某种风投可投的东西之间的鸿沟。但那通常是一个五六年的鸿沟,而且被填补得很糟糕。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: And tell me a little bit more about the idea. So they come from a bunch of different places, but what does an idea look like in its rawest form? Is it like Waymo or a self driving car? Was that the idea, or was it, you know what I mean? What do they look like at that stage?
zh: 那再多讲讲想法本身。它们来自很多不同的地方,但一个想法在最原始的形态下是什么样子?是像 Waymo 或自动驾驶汽车那样吗?那就是那个想法吗,还是,你懂我意思吧?在那个阶段它们长什么样?

speaker: Astro Teller
en: So the ideas come from all over the world. In the very early days, Waymo said, more than a million people die in car accidents. It makes no sense that humans are still driving cars. A moonshot for us is huge problem with the world, science fiction sounding solution to that problem, and some technology or set of technologies that give us a sense that this is a testable hypothesis for making that science fiction sounding solution. So Waymo said in the early days, more than a million people die in car accidents every year. More than a trillion dollars is wasted in car accidents and people sitting in traffic. That is not the future. Crazy idea, what if cars just drove themselves and we're just going to make a self driving car. And here's a set of reasons to believe that the technology, LIDAR, radar, et cetera, is just ready enough. This was like circa 2009, 2010, that maybe we could do it. We'll be the right amount too early in trying to do that. But even then, saying we're making a self driving car turned out to be the wrong framing. I mean, it got us going. But after a while, we realized, oh, we're not actually trying to make and sell cars. That's not our job. So if the first five years Waymo thought we're going to be making and selling a car. The next five years they thought, actually our job is transforming mobility, just moving people from point A to point B, that's our job. But even that framing, while better was still wrong. Because do we really want to be the ones cleaning the cars? Do we want to be the ones charging the cars? Do we want necessarily to have to own the interface with the consumer on their phone? And so if you ask Waymo now, what's your framing for what you're doing? They say they're trying to make the world's safest driver and so, by getting more and more specific. Obviously the world's safest driver was a part of making a self driving car. But as they're getting more and more concrete, and specific about what they want to be the best in the world at. It opens up more possibilities for them to explore that space differently, to partner better with other people and that's part of the learning journey of a moonshot, is trying to understand the sort of architecture for where we're going, why we're going there, what kind of help we need along the way. How to understand what it means when the alligators jump out of the swamp and try to bite us.
zh: 这些想法来自世界各地。在很早的时候,Waymo 说,每年有一百多万人死于车祸。人类还在开汽车这件事毫无道理。对我们来说,一个登月项目是世界上巨大的问题、听起来像科幻小说的问题解决方案,以及某种技术或一组技术,让我们感觉到这是让那个听起来像科幻小说的解决方案成为一个可检验假设的途径。所以 Waymo 早期说,每年有一百多万人死于车祸。超过一万亿美元被浪费在车祸和人们坐在交通堵塞里。那不是未来。疯狂的想法,如果汽车自己开动呢,我们就是要造一辆自动驾驶汽车。这里有一组理由让我们相信技术,LIDAR、雷达等等,已经足够就绪。这大概是 2009、2010 年左右,也许我们能做到。我们在尝试做这件事时会「早得恰到好处」。但即便如此,说我们要造自动驾驶汽车结果被证明是错误的框架。我是说,它让我们动起来了。但过了一段时间,我们意识到,哦,我们其实不是要造车和卖车。那不是我们的工作。所以如果头五年 Waymo 认为我们要造车和卖车。接下来的五年他们认为,其实我们的工作是变革出行,只是把人从 A 点移动到 B 点,那是我们的工作。但即便那个框架,虽然更好,仍然是错的。因为我们真的想成为擦车的人吗?我们想成为给车充电的人吗?我们有必要非得拥有手机上与消费者的界面吗?所以如果你现在问 Waymo,你们对所做事情的框架是什么?他们会说他们在努力成为世界上最安全的司机,而且,通过变得越来越具体。显然,世界上最安全的司机是造自动驾驶汽车的一部分。但随着他们对自己想成为世界最好的那个领域越来越具体、越来越明确,它为他们打开了更多可能性,以不同的方式探索那个空间,更好地与其他人合作,而这也是登月项目学习旅程的一部分:试图理解我们要去哪里的架构,我们为什么去那里,一路上我们需要什么样的帮助。以及如何理解当鳄鱼从沼泽里跳出来试图咬我们时,这意味着什么。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: And would you say, take Waymo for example. It's a type of idea which I would categorize as, if you build it, they will come. If you can actually deliver self driving and you figure out the logistics and you figure out the price, obviously. But many people are going to want to not drive their car because many people want a driver. Are most of your ideas like that where it's, will the tech get there, and that's kind of the main risk? Or is that just, that just happens to be Waymo, but others are more. Maybe the tech is there and now it's a demand risk or the risk is somewhere else other than just, can we build it?
zh: 你会怎么说,拿 Waymo 举例。它是一种我会归类为,if you build it, they will come 的想法。如果你真的能实现自动驾驶,而且你搞定了物流,而且你搞定了价格,显然。但很多人会想要不开自己的车,因为很多人想要一个司机。你的大多数想法都是那样的吗,即技术能不能到达那里,那是主要风险?还是说那只是恰好是 Waymo,而其他的是更多。也许技术已经在了,现在是需求风险,或者风险在别的地方,而不仅仅是,我们能不能造出来?

speaker: Astro Teller
en: We always will lean harder on the sort of technical, operational, like, how do you pull this all together? We won't lean particularly hard, the dominant risk couldn't be kind of public policy and government relations. We do that, but that shouldn't be the dominant risk. It shouldn't be a marketing risk. If we have to just make people want this thing more than something fairly equivalent, that's just not what we should be world class at. But I'll give you an example where it wasn't just a tech risk. Google Glass, turns out we were to too early there. But increasingly, it's looking like we were very right. The whole world has come back around to that. But when we made it, we were trying to figure out, we have a sense that people want to get away from their phones. I think it now turns out we were right, but we were also too early and just saying people want to get away from their phones doesn't mean you can necessarily make it feasibly. But also, how to land that with consumers and with society so that people understand it and feel good about it. There was a lot that was hard, and it was a learning journey for us. And we got some things very right, but we also were too early and got some things wrong. So maybe that's an example that's not like Waymo. We couldn't prove ahead of time, if we can make it, this will win.
zh: 我们总是会更强地偏向那种技术性的、运营性的,像,你怎么把这一切整合起来?我们不会特别偏向,主导风险不能是公共政策或政府关系那种。我们做那些,但那不应该是主导风险。它不应该是一个营销风险。如果我们只是得让人们比另一个相当等价的东西更想要这个东西,那不应该是我们应该世界顶尖的事情。但我给你一个例子,它不只是技术风险。Google Glass,结果发现我们太,太早了。但现在越来越明显的是,我们当时非常正确。整个世界已经回到了那个方向上。但当我们做它的时候,我们试图搞清楚,我们有一种感觉,人们想要逃离他们的手机。我觉得现在看来我们是对的,但我们也太早了,而仅仅说人们想逃离手机并不意味着你 necessarily 能把它做出来。还有,如何让它落地到消费者和社会,让人们理解它并且对它感觉良好。有很多难的地方,而这对我们来说是一段学习旅程。我们有些地方非常正确,但我们也太早了,而且有些地方做错了。所以也许这是一个不像 Waymo 的例子。我们无法提前证明,如果我们能做出来,它就会赢。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: So tell me about the next layer of filtering. That's where all the ideas come from. Even just picking the next, two hundred you're going to work on this year. What's that process like?
zh: 那跟我说说下一层过滤。想法就是从那些地方来的。光是挑选你们今年要做的下两百个。那个过程是什么样的?

speaker: Astro Teller
en: Often things will not make it to that sort of, the ones that get a code name. Because nobody believes in it strongly enough to spend at least fifty percent of their time on it. People can't describe it crisply in terms of those three things I just described. Huge problem with the world, radical proposed solution, breakthrough technology. Where it feels like now there's something there. But sometimes people, for example, will say what it is, but they haven't figured out how to make it a testable hypothesis and you saying, hey, the world might be like this in the future, is like, yeah, you might be right. But that's not what we do. We do not fund things for five years so you can go try it. We're going to fund this for like five weeks, maybe five months. Which is easy for us because you're part of X, right? We don't have to incorporate anything and you're almost certainly wrong. So spend the next month or two trying to get one piece of information that tells us whether you're a little bit more wrong than we think or a little bit less wrong than we think. But if you don't have a testable hypothesis, we can't even get onto that flywheel. So that's another reason. Sometimes someone will have a really interesting proposal, but we just don't have the right labs for it, and we can't find someone who does, or sometimes something will go dormant because we're like, hey, that's a really cool idea. We need this physical lab. Hey, Caltech has that lab, and then we end up spending a year in slow motion just working with some university to have them let us use their lab. So then we're spending almost no time on that, just sort of waiting for the contract to come through and then it comes back to life. So very different reasons. But ultimately, the question is never, I have to prove, as the captain of Moonshots, that your idea is physically impossible. Almost nothing is physically impossible. It's actually more like you have to prove that your idea has a better reward risk ratio than the other things that we're currently looking at, and I would actually say it's reward divided by risk. Which includes all the costs and time, relative to how cheap or expensive it is to answer each question about, hey, what did we learn this week? Hey, what did we learn this week? If the reward risk ratio is okay, and it's going to take us a million dollars to find out the first piece of information about whether we're on the right track, not worth it. Reward is ginormous, risk is pretty big but we can find out for $100,000 whether this is a little bit less crazy than we thought. Yeah, I'll play that game all day long.
zh: 通常有些东西到不了那个拿到代号的阶段。因为没有人足够强烈地相信它,愿意把至少百分之五十的时间花在上面。人们无法用我刚才描述的那三样东西把它清晰地描述出来。世界上巨大的问题、激进的提议解决方案、突破性技术。然后才感觉现在这里有点东西。但有时人们,比如,能说出它是什么,但他们还没搞清楚怎么把它变成一个可检验的假设,而你说,嘿,未来世界也许会是这样,对方说,嗯,你可能是对的。但那不是我们做的事。我们不会为一个东西资助五年让你去试。我们只会资助这个大概五周,也许五个月。这对我们来说很容易,因为你是 X 的一部分,对吧?我们不必注册任何公司,而且你几乎肯定是错的。所以花接下来的一两个月,努力搞到一条信息,它告诉我们你是比我们以为的更错一点,还是没那么错一点。但如果你没有一个可检验的假设,我们连那个飞轮都上不去。所以那是另一个原因。有时某人会有一个非常有趣的提案,但我们就是没有合适的实验室,我们也找不到有实验室的人,或者有时某个东西会休眠,因为我们说,嘿,那真是个很酷的想法。我们需要这个实体实验室。嘿,Caltech 有那个实验室,然后我们最后花一年时间慢动作般地和某所大学合作,让他们让我们用他们的实验室。然后那段时间我们几乎不在上面花时间,就等着合同走完,然后它又复活了。所以原因非常不同。但最终,问题从来不是,作为登月项目的船长,我必须证明你的想法在物理上不可能。几乎没有什么是物理上不可能的。实际上更像是,你必须证明你的想法比我们目前正在看的其他东西有更好的回报风险比,而我实际上会说它是回报除以风险。其中包含所有的成本和时间,相对于回答每个关于「嘿,我们这周学到了什么?」的问题有多便宜或昂贵。如果回报风险比还可以,而要搞清楚我们是否在正轨上的第一条信息要花一百万美元,不值。回报巨大,风险挺大,但我们可以花十万美元搞清楚这是不是比我们以为的没那么疯狂一点。行,这个游戏我愿意玩一整天。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: I'm going to ask you for a small favor, a tiny little favor. In fact, now that I think about it. It's not even really a favor for me. I'm actually trying to help you do a favor for you. Just hit the follow button. You won't miss out on the next episode. You'll see everything that we release. If you don't want to listen to an episode, you just skip it. But at least you don't miss out. Tell me a bit about that next step, maybe give me an example of this testable hypothesis. Because I think that's a huge learning for founders. A lot of founders are not like me, by the way, and they have many ideas. A lot of ideas, and what they're not good at is, how do I kill it? How do I, as quickly as possible, in a week, two weeks, four weeks max. Kill it, move on to the next one, and go all in on the thing that actually shows the most promise. A subset of what you're doing.
zh: 我要请你帮个小忙,一个小小的忙。事实上,现在我想想。这其实根本算不上帮我的忙。我其实是在帮你帮你一个忙。就点一下关注按钮。你就不会错过下一期。你会看到我们发布的所有内容。如果你不想听某一期,你就跳过它。但至少你不会错过。跟我说说下一步,也许给我一个这种可检验假设的例子。因为我觉得这对创始人是一个巨大的学习。顺便说,很多创始人不像我,他们有很多想法。很多很多想法,而他们不擅长的是,我怎么杀掉它?我怎么,尽快地,在一周、两周、最多四周内。杀掉它,转向下一个,然后 all in 在真正展现出最大希望的那个东西上。你所做事情的一个子集。

speaker: Astro Teller
en: I'll give you an example, but first, bear with me for a very short story. Because this is how we talk about it here at X. So for a long time, I would say to Xers, obviously, we should work on the riskiest part of the problem first and pretty much everybody at X said, I'm pretty sure that's wrong, Astro. And I said, no, that's what we should do. And we just were not connecting on this. And then, I was at a Wall Street Journal live conference about eleven years ago on stage, and I said, we obviously should work on the riskiest part of the problem first. And the interviewer said, I'm pretty sure that's right. I don't think that's right. What do you mean? So in a moment of hyperbole, I said, look, let's say that our collective project was to get a monkey to stand on the top of a 10-foot pedestal and recite Shakespeare. Which should we do first in this somewhat extreme situation? Build the pedestal or train the monkey? In this extreme situation, we can see that if you built the pedestal, you're half done but you're really zero percent done at burning down the risk.
zh: 我给你一个例子,但首先,容我讲一个非常短的故事。因为这就是我们在 X 谈论它的方式。很长一段时间,我会对 Xer 说,显然,我们应该先做问题中风险最大的部分,而 X 里几乎所有人都会说,我相当确定那是错的,Astro。而我说,不,那就是我们该做的。而我们就是没有在这个点上对上频道。然后,大概十一年前,我在一个华尔街日报的现场会议上在台上,我说,我们显然应该先做问题中风险最大的部分。采访者说,我相当确定那是对的。我不认为那是对的。你什么意思?于是在一个夸张的时刻,我说,听着,假设我们的集体任务是让一只猴子站在十英尺高的基座顶上背诵莎士比亚。在这种有些极端的情况下,我们应该先做哪件事?搭基座还是训练猴子?在这种极端情况下,我们可以看到,如果你搭好了基座,你完成了一半,但在消解风险上你实际上是百分之零。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: That's right.
zh: 没错。

speaker: Astro Teller
en: The point of a testable hypothesis, especially at X. Everyone at X will just say as shorthand to each other, what's the monkey? What they mean by that is not just, do you have a testable hypothesis but how is the thing that you're doing now attempting to burn down the risk on the riskiest part of the problem? Because if you can't train the monkey, you do not need to build the pedestal, obviously, and in a much more subtle way for every moonshot we have here. How scary is making this thing physically? Oh yeah, if we're really honest, we're going to be able to do it. How cheaply can we make it? Oh yeah, that actually could be the scary part. Okay, if the scary part is the techno economics. Let's not wait. Let's get really crisp about what has to be true. Maybe you can just do a bunch of spreadsheet math and kill the project on the basis of, okay, almost no matter how good we make each of these ten pieces. We're going to have to jam them all together. Yeah, the numbers are just not going to pencil out. This is not going to be competitive. Great, kill the project, move on. Sometimes it's actually how people will use something. Sometimes it's a safety issue and sometimes the solutions. In the very early days of Wing, we spent so much time trying to think about safety and make it safe with a very small number of propellers.
zh: 可检验假设的重点,尤其是在 X。X 里的每个人都会用速记彼此说,猴子是什么?他们的意思不只是,你有没有一个可检验假设,而是你现在做的事情如何试图消解问题中风险最大那部分的风险?因为如果你训练不了猴子,你就不需要搭基座,显然,而且以一种更微妙的方式适用于我们这里的每一个登月项目。把这个东西物理上造出来有多吓人?哦,是的,如果我们真的诚实,我们能造出来。我们能把它造得多便宜?哦,是的,那其实可能才是吓人的部分。好,如果吓人的部分是技术经济学。那我们就别等了。我们来把「什么必须为真」弄得非常清晰。也许你只要做一堆表格数学就能杀掉这个项目,依据是,好,几乎无论我们把这十个部件中的每一个做得多好。我们都得把它们全部拼在一起。对,数字就是算不过来。这不会有竞争力。好,杀掉项目,继续前进。有时它其实是人们会怎么使用某个东西。有时是安全问题,有时是解决方案本身。在 Wing 非常早期的时候,我们花了非常多时间思考安全,并且用非常少的螺旋桨把它做安全。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: And Wing, for those who don't know, that's the drone delivery.
zh: 而 Wing,给那些不知道的人,那是无人机配送。

speaker: Astro Teller
en: Drones for package delivery. Until we got to the place where we said, what are we doing? These are literally hobbyist motors. They don't cost us that much. What if we just had a bunch extra? Then if a blade falls off, some motor stops working in the middle of a flight, we won't even notice. So safety was still really important. But all of a sudden, safety moved from being this complex control problem to something where for a very small incremental cost. We were just over actuated and then we had this defense in depth. And so safety then dropped as a risk. And then there were all kinds of other risks that we had to work on.
zh: 送包裹的无人机。直到我们到达那个我们说,我们在干嘛?这些 literally 是航模爱好者的马达。它们花不了我们多少钱。如果我们多装一批呢?那么如果一个桨叶掉了,某个马达在飞行中途停了,我们甚至不会注意到。所以安全仍然真的很重要。但突然间,安全从一个复杂的控制问题变成了一个只需很小的增量成本的东西。我们只是超量驱动了,然后我们有了这种纵深防御。于是安全作为一个风险降下去了。然后还有各种其他风险需要我们去做。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: So you find the biggest risk and you try and de-risk that. And if I understood you correctly earlier, if the biggest risk is going to take too much time, too much money to de-risk. That alone is a reason for moving on to the next one.
zh: 所以你找到最大的风险,然后试着给那个去风险。而如果我之前理解得对的话,如果最大的风险要花太多时间、太多钱去消解。那本身就是转向下一个的理由。

speaker: Astro Teller
en: Yeah, but if you have a crazy idea about nuclear fusion. Okay, first, let's see if we can kill it on the whiteboard. If we can't kill it on the whiteboard, I guarantee you the next thing we're doing is not building something the size of a house to start doing plasma shots. We're going to build a simulator or find someone who has a simulator and see if we can kill it using the simulator. If it survives that process, maybe we have to build something the size of a house, but maybe we can even find someone in a university who can do a little bit of the de-risking with us even if it's only bits and pieces. And then when we get to the place, which we did. We closed this down about a year and a half ago. We had a fusion project. We ran it. We did build something the size of a house. We did almost a thousand plasma shots. We convinced ourself it was not going to change the world, and we closed the project down. But it was money well spent because we had removed all the cheaper ways to try that first. Speaking of which, we have a Moonshot podcast. If your audience wants to hear more about some of these stories. Really hear what it was like building Waymo or building Wing. Building this Fusion project. We now have two seasons out. If people just search for Moonshot Factory Moonshot podcast, it'll come up and I think people really enjoy this sort of deep dives. It's not just what it was like for us, but it's exploring with the entrepreneurs that have gone through X. What it felt like for them and what other people can learn about taking their own shots.
zh: 是的,但如果你有一个关于核聚变的疯狂想法。好,首先,让我们看看能不能在白板上杀掉它。如果我们不能在白板上杀掉它,我向你保证,我们接下来要做的绝不是造一个房子那么大的东西开始做等离子体射击。我们会造一个模拟器,或者找一个有模拟器的人,看看能不能用模拟器杀掉它。如果它在那之后存活下来,也许我们得造一个房子那么大的东西,但也许我们甚至能在大学里找到能和我们一起做一点点去风险的人,哪怕只有零星几块。然后当我们到达那个地方——我们确实到了。我们在大约一年半前关掉了这个项目。我们有一个聚变项目。我们运行了它。我们确实造了房子那么大的东西。我们做了差不多一千次等离子体射击。我们说服了自己它不会改变世界,然后我们关掉了项目。但那些钱花得值,因为我们已经先排除了所有更便宜的尝试方式。说到这个,我们有一个登月播客。如果你的听众想听更多这些故事。真正听听建 Waymo 或建 Wing 是什么样的。建这个聚变项目是什么样。我们现在已经出了两季。如果人们搜索 Moonshot Factory Moonshot podcast,就会出来,我觉得人们真的很喜欢这种深挖。它不只是对我们来说是什么样,而是和那些经历过 X 的创业者一起探索。对他们来说是什么感觉,以及其他人在进行自己的尝试时能学到什么。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: So we've talked through a few steps, how we come up with the ideas, how you start killing them off as quickly as possible by finding the main risk. What's the next step after that?
zh: 我们已经聊过了几个步骤,我们怎么想出这些想法,你怎么通过找到主要风险尽快开始杀掉它们。那之后下一步是什么?

speaker: Astro Teller
en: I mean, this sounds a little bit extreme but there is no step after that. You just keep doing that. If you do that for six years and you've burned down a lot of the risk. If we're actually at the place where we're like, well, there's a sizable chance this actually could be a Waymo someday. Then it graduates from X and, often this is sort of on the order of ten to fifty people who leave to set up this new business. No one makes anyone leave X. If you want to stay and you have to find a new job, a new thing to do at X, that's cool. If you're excited about the teleporter and it looks like it's really working and you're going to get a non-trivial amount of shares in the teleporter company. You better believe in it because you're about to start getting paid in illiquid stock now instead of paid like a Googler. Then it's an independent business and you guys are off to the races. But until then we structure everything in terms of, what are we learning here? In fact, the baby board meetings that we have for the more mature projects are called quarterly learning reviews. Just to remind everybody, don't show me your progress. Progress is like a smoke screen. That's the rowing frantically in the ocean thing. What we want to know is, what have you really learned? Because if you have spent five or six years at X and you graduate with like Series A, maybe even seed stage Product Market Fit. We are totally fine with that, because you will have tried six or seven times to figure out what the right best connection point to the world is. We don't want a Product Market Fit. We want this sort of moonshot market fit, which is much more holistic. Often we're trying to change a system out in the world. So finding some little thing that people will buy, which in some sense is a product market fit. Actually doesn't have a very good chance of changing the system. If our real goal is to fix the system, then we have to figure out a much more complex set of things.
zh: 我是说,这听起来有点极端,但那之后没有下一步了。你就是继续那么做。如果你那样做了六年,并且消解了大量的风险。如果我们真的到了那个地方,我们觉得,嗯,有相当大的机会这个东西有一天真的能成为 Waymo。那它就从 X 毕业,而且,通常这是大概十到五十个人离开去创办这个新业务。没有人强迫任何人离开 X。如果你想留下,你得找一份新工作、在 X 找一件新的事做,那没问题。如果你对传送机感到兴奋,而且它看起来真的在起作用,而你会得到传送机公司一笔不小的股份。你最好相信它,因为你即将开始以非流动性股票获得报酬,而不是像 Googler 那样拿报酬。那它就是一项独立业务,你们就大展宏图了。但在那之前,我们以「我们在这里学到了什么」来构建一切。事实上,我们为更成熟的项目开的那些 baby board 会议,叫做季度学习回顾。就是为了提醒每个人,别给我看你的进展。进展就像一层烟幕。那是Ocean 上疯狂划桨的事情。我们想知道的是,你们真正学到了什么?因为如果你在 X 花了五六年,毕业时有 Series A,也许甚至 seed 阶段的 Product Market Fit。我们完全可以接受,因为你会已经试了六七次去搞清楚什么是正确的、最好的与世界的连接点。我们不想要一个 Product Market Fit。我们想要这种登月市场匹配,它是整体得多的。通常我们是在试图改变世界上的一个系统。所以找到某个人们会买的小东西,这在某种意义上是一种 product market fit。实际上并没有很大的机会去改变那个系统。如果我们真正的目标是修复这个系统,那我们就得搞清楚一个复杂得多的集合。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Tell me more about, I want to go deeper on killing ideas and it gets harder, and harder. I assume as you progress through them, maybe whether it's through examples or maybe you have a process for making these decision points. I'm curious exactly how that works, because I think, again, that's another huge piece of learning for most founders who are very blinders on. This thing must work at all costs and I've just seen it so many times where, honestly, five years later. Seven years down the line, and you might actually have a few million in revenue but it's a bit of a zombie company. And in hindsight, 2020, it just feels like, you know what, you might've been able to see this five years ago. So I'm curious what kind of process you have for figuring that out.
zh: 跟我多讲讲,我想更深入地聊杀掉想法这件事,它会越来越难,越来越难。我猜随着你在其中推进,也许通过例子,也许你们有一个做这些决策点的流程。我很好奇那到底是怎么运作的,因为我觉得,再说一次,对大多数戴着眼罩、认为这东西必须不惜一切代价成功的创始人来说,这是又一大块学习。而我见过太多次,老实说,五年之后。七年过去了,你可能实际上有几百万营收,但它是一家有点僵尸的公司。而事后诸葛亮,2020,就是感觉,你知道吗,你也许五年前就能看出来。所以我很好奇你们有什么样的流程来搞清楚这个。

speaker: Astro Teller
en: Yeah, I'm going to describe it, but just first to be fair to entrepreneurs. There's a bit of a mentality in the venture world with entrepreneurs. I want you as an investor to burn your boats at the shore. So that you and your men fight like crazy to take Troy or whatever city you're trying to capture. Because I know if you burn your boats at the shore, you will just fight harder and that's true. The question is, did you pick the right city to burn your boats in front of? But once you've burned your boats, asking that question is just kind of scary because there isn't really a way back. You can give the remaining money back to the investors. But I just want to recognize to entrepreneurs who are listening to this, before we talk about how to kill your project. A lot of it is about the incentive structures. If they're not put into a situation where it's in their best interest to give money back to the investors and call it a day. It just kind of won't and that doesn't make them stupid. It's like the system has not helped them feel it. Now what you just pointed out is really important, which is, it's their life that's ticking away. So that actually by itself should be worth it to do, but often it's not. So for us we will do a set of things, but here's one that we do all the time. We insist on it, it's called kill criteria. So if your project has moved past the investigation stage, now a few of you are going to be full time on this thing. We're tracking the costs. It's probably not public yet. There might only be three or four of you full time on the project, but given all the resources around X you can borrow. You're probably acting like maybe a ten person company at this point. Right at that moment where you start to do this full time, write down your kill criteria. This is like an honesty message from you to your future self. At some point, call it a year in the future, the following things should be true. This is what I, current Astro, think are the monkeys. We have to be able to do at least A, B, and C at least this well for each of them. In order for us to be taking this project seriously and of course, at that moment, I'm going to be feeling so cocky and everything's going to be great. So I'm going to set A and B and C. I'll try to sandbag a little bit, but entrepreneurs are never realistic enough.
zh: 是的,我会描述它,但首先为了对创业者公平。风投圈对创业者有一种心态。我要你作为投资人在岸边烧掉你的船。这样你和你的部下会拼命作战去攻下特洛伊或你想攻占的任何城市。因为我知道如果你在岸边烧掉你的船,你就会战斗得更狠,那是真的。问题是,你有没有选对烧船的城市?但一旦你烧掉了你的船,问那个问题就有点吓人了,因为其实没有回头路。你可以把剩下的钱还给投资人。但我只是想向正在听这个的创业者们说明,在我们聊怎么杀掉你的项目之前。其中很多关乎激励结构。如果他们没有被放进一个「把钱还给投资人然后收摊是对他们最有利的」的处境。他们就是不会,而这并不让他们愚蠢。而是这个系统没有帮他们感受到它。而你刚才指出的真的很重要,那就是,是他们的人生在流逝。所以那件事本身就应该值得去做,但常常不是。所以对我们来说,我们会做一组事情,但这里有一个我们一直在做的。我们坚持要求,它叫做 kill criteria,即终止标准。所以如果你的项目已经过了调查阶段,现在你们几个人要全职投入这个事了。我们在追踪成本。它可能还没公开。也许只有三四个人全职在项目上,但鉴于 X 周围你可以借用的所有资源。你此刻可能表现得像一家十人左右的公司。就在你开始全职做这件事的那一刻,写下你的终止标准。这是你给未来的自己的一条诚实讯息。在某个时点,比如说未来一年,以下这些事情应该为真。这是我,现在的 Astro,认为的猴子。我们必须至少能做到 A、B、C,每一项至少达到这个水平。为了让我们继续认真对待这个项目。当然,在那一刻,我会感觉非常自信,一切都会很棒。所以我会定下 A、B、C。我会试着稍微放点水,但创业者从来都不够现实。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: What's an example of some of those A, B, C? That's a revenue milestone, I assume. So what might that be?
zh: 那些A、B、C的例子是什么？我猜那是营收里程碑。那可能会是什么？

speaker: Astro Teller
en: If you want to make a magic box that pulls clean water from the air. Let's say, just using sunlight, which we did. By the way, and talked about on the podcast. Then let's agree, after a year of this, you're still going to have a super rough prototype. So you will not have scaled, but you need to be able to tell a fairly exciting and specific story about how we're going to get down to a penny a liter. Because at 10 cents a liter, it's glamping, it's kind of cool, but it won't really change the world. At a penny a liter, you will change the lives of more than a billion people on planet Earth, super exciting. Can we agree that within a year you need to be able to tell that story about what the techno economic slope is like? And you have the next year to go figure all of that out.
zh: 假设你想造一个从空气中提取清洁水的魔法盒子。比如，只用阳光，顺便说一句，我们做过这个，还在播客上聊过。那我们约定，一年之后，你仍然会只有一个非常粗糙的原型。所以你不会有规模化的东西，但你需要能讲出一个相当令人兴奋且具体的故事，讲我们如何把成本降到每升一美分。因为在每升十美分的时候，那是豪华露营，挺酷的，但不会真正改变世界。在每升一美分的时候，你将改变地球上超过十亿人的生活，非常令人兴奋。我们能否达成一致：一年之内你需要能讲出那个关于技术经济曲线是什么样的故事？然后你有接下来的一年去把这一切搞清楚。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Not even do it, by the way, just have a very clear, sharp story about it.
zh: 顺便说一句，甚至不用做到，只需要对此有一个非常清晰、犀利的story。

speaker: Astro Teller
en: Tell a really clear story about it and that seems like, yeah, sure, that seems fair. You're not asking me to have something in manufacturing and then a year later. We sit down and talk, and you don't have that story. Doesn't mean we have to kill the project, but the default is we're going to kill the project. So then I say to you, if you're working on this, look, I know you're excited about it, Pablo. I want to make the clean water for the world, too. But we pre agreed that this was kind of the monkey. You don't have a really good answer to this. Why would we continue it in the absence of that really good answer? What else have you learned that makes this worth us taking another shot at it?
zh: 讲一个非常清晰的故事，这听起来，是的，当然，那看起来是公平的。你不是在要求我一年后就有东西进入制造阶段。我们坐下来谈，而你没有那个故事。这不意味着我们必须砍掉项目，但默认是我们要砍掉项目。于是我对你说，如果你在做这个，听着，我知道你很兴奋，Pablo。我也想为世界制造清洁水。但我们事先约定过这就是那只猴子。你没有对此的真正好答案。在没有那个真正好答案的情况下，我们为什么要继续？你还学到了什么别的东西，让这值得我们再试一次？

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: And that decision, by the way. Because I think that's important, is you and them agree, or just you have the veto right there. What is that structure like?
zh: 顺便说一句，那个决定，因为我觉得这很重要，是你和他们一起同意，还是只有你拥有否决权。那个结构是什么样的？

speaker: Astro Teller
en: You'd be surprised, I have had to insist. I don't make up the kill criteria. I want you to make the kill criteria because I want you to own it, right? If you think that you're working on the teleporter and fundamentally you want the teleporter to win more badly than you want to be a great Xer, card counter of innovation. You and I are not on the same team, and then I'll probably kill the teleporter just on the basis of you as the lead not being on the same team with me. Once we agree that it's more important to find the truth than for you to keep the teleporter alive. You tell me, I want the truth, and so do you. We're trying to figure out how to maximize goodness that we can create for the world over the next one or two decades. Is this really that? Tell me a story. Tell me, get specific and if you do it right, which at least to some extent I think we have at X. There's a microcosm that makes it kind of uncomfortable to be salesy and partisan on the behalf of the thing that you're locally trying to work on. Because everyone else here just would think that was gross. But that's an expectation that you have to wire into the culture and constantly reinforce because that's not how the rest of the world works.
zh: 你会感到惊讶，我不得不坚持这一点。制定淘汰标准的人不是我。我要你来制定淘汰标准，因为我要你拥有它，对吧？如果你认为你在做那个传送机，而且从根本上说，你希望传送机获胜的愿望，比你希望成为一个伟大的Xer、创新的算牌者更强烈。那你和我就不在同一个团队，那我可能仅凭你作为负责人不与我同队这一点就会砍掉传送机。一旦我们同意找到真相比保住传送机更重要。你告诉我，我要真相，你也要真相。我们在试图弄清楚如何最大化我们在未来一二十年能为世界创造的善。这真的是那个吗？给我讲个故事。讲给我听，说具体点，如果你做对了——至少在某种程度上我认为我们在X做到了——会有一个微观环境，让你为你手头正在做的东西做推销式、党派式的辩护会变得有点不舒服。因为这里的其他人都会觉得那很恶心。但这是一个你必须植入文化并不断强化期望，因为世界其他地方不是这样运作的。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: And is that, you mentioned a year. Is that the standard or sometimes it's like a month? That kill criteria framework.
zh: 那这个，你提到了一年。那是标准吗，还是有时候是一个月？那个淘汰标准框架。

speaker: Astro Teller
en: Yeah, I mean there's a group here working on something super unlikely to work. Absolutely would change the world if it did, and they said, hey, we think we could try this in six months for like $100,000. And I said, you know what, the reward risk ratio here is good. And those two people who started this new project, are the two people who by themselves killed off the fusion project. They made a two hundred and fifty page slide deck about why we should close it down. I didn't do that, and so then they built their credibility that they're intellectually honest. So when they came with this pretty crazy sounding idea, I said, okay. Now, that was nine months ago. Project's not dead. After six months, we were starting to get some data. Shocker, it was inconclusive. Could be really good. We're still chasing it. It'll probably be a year and $200,000 till we really learn on that one. But that's okay. That's still pretty cheap if it's really a Waymo, Google Brain size thing. If it happens to work out, and of course, there would be a decade of work afterwards if it did work out. It's not like we would be done. But that's not the question. The question is, how much of the risk can you burn down cheaply?
zh: 是的，这里有一个团队在做一件非常不太可能成功的事。如果成功了绝对会改变世界，他们说，嘿，我们觉得我们可以用大概十万美元在六个月内试试这个。我说，你们知道吗，这里的回报风险比是不错的。而启动这个新项目的两个人，正是当年仅凭他们自己就砍掉了核聚变项目的人。他们做了一份两百五十页的幻灯片，讲为什么我们应该关掉它。那不是我做的，于是他们建立了自己智识上诚实的信誉。所以当他们带着这个听起来相当疯狂的想法来找我时，我说，好吧。那是九个月前的事了。项目没死。六个月之后，我们开始拿到一些数据。意外吧，结论是不确定的。可能会非常好。我们还在追。在那件事上真正学到东西大概还要一年和二十万美元。但这没关系。如果它真的是一个Waymo、Google Brain规模的东西，这仍然相当便宜。如果它碰巧成功了，当然，之后还会有十年的工作。不是说我我们就完事了。但那不是问题。问题是，你能用多低的成本烧掉多少风险？

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: And this is a bit of an outside question, but I'm curious if you have any thoughts about it. Are people working in person? Are they working remote? Do you find that makes a difference to the speed of execution on these ideas?
zh: 这是个有点题外的问题，但我好奇你对此有没有什么想法。人们是在现场工作吗？还是远程工作？你发现这对执行这些想法的速度有影响吗？

speaker: Astro Teller
en: I try to be really open minded about a lot of things. So what I've said to Xers is, I just want us to be efficient. But this is a creativity factory, even more than it's a technology factory and so far, I've seen no evidence that we can be at our creative best when we're remote from each other. I think people work somewhat less hard, but they also work in much more siloed ways and creativity is usually not about my idea or your idea. It's about the sparks that happen when our ideas clash. That's where the real value is and our ideas won't clash effectively when we're all just typing in our bedrooms. So, of course, every Xer here will occasionally take some time at home. If you have heads down things you need to do, no reason to do a commute. But Xers spend the bulk of their time here, and I think that's pretty critical. Plus, it's just more fun. Commutes suck, but being together is more fun. I think it still nets to the positive, if you have a great work environment.
zh: 我在很多事情上都尽量保持非常开放的心态。所以我对Xer们说的是，我只想要我们高效。但这是一座创造力工厂，甚至超过它是一座技术工厂，而到目前为止，我没有看到任何证据表明我们在彼此远离时能处于创造力的最佳状态。我认为人们工作得没那么卖力，而且他们还以更加孤岛化的方式工作，而创造力通常不是关于我的想法或你的想法。它是关于当我们的想法碰撞时产生的火花。那才是真正的价值所在，而当我们都只是在各自卧室里打字时，我们的想法不会有效地碰撞。所以，当然，这里的每个Xer都会偶尔在家待一段时间。如果你有需要埋头做的事情，没理由去通勤。但Xer们把大部分时间花在这里，我认为这相当关键。另外，就是更有趣。通勤很糟，但在一起更有趣。我觉得如果你有一个很好的工作环境，这仍然是净正收益。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: This is the Product Market Fit Show. So I'll maybe end it and we can talk a little bit about this, especially because you've seen so many ideas. What is Product Market Fit to you? You mentioned moonshot market fit. So maybe talk about that, but what does real pull for an idea look like to you?
zh: 这是Product Market Fit Show。所以也许我可以以此收尾，我们可以稍微聊聊这个，尤其是因为你已经见过这么多想法。Product Market Fit对你来说是什么？你提到了moonshot market fit。所以也许谈谈那个，但对你来说，一个想法真正的拉力是什么样的？

speaker: Astro Teller
en: I think some people think of Product Market Fit as, are people paying me for it? That's a super low bar. Are the right kind of people paying me for it? That's a slightly higher bar. Are they paying me more for it than it costs for me to make the thing? That's a slightly higher bar. How expensive is it for me to find these people and talk them into buying it, as opposed to their coming and finding me? Where are we on the spectrum from hard push to easy pull? And that stuff matters, but if you're trying to live to fight another day. Maybe that basket of things is mostly it. There's some other stuff in product, like how easy is it for a distributor to explain this to somebody when you're not there? That's pretty important in a real finished product. But at X, we're focused more on things like, what are the acupressure points in the industry? Or if, for example, we have a moonshot for the electric grid. But you cannot make a fake little grid in your lab and learn anything. And you can't start by going to these grid operators and saying, give me all your data, I'm going to do a little thing for you. This is a national security thing for every country in the world. They're just not going to do it. We spent five years doing things that would help us deeply understand their problems. So that we could start helping them and the first couple of things we did weren't even the moonshot. It was just getting a rapport going so that we could, with the grid operators of the world, start to move their grid operations and planning, and optimization into the 21st century. But we put in five, six years of work that was not product focused but looked a little bit like product focus but it wasn't Product Market Fit. Because that's not what, we were actually trying to fit with the partners so that we could get into a rhythm with them. So that we could then build things that would solve their problems. That's an example of what feels like moonshot market fit to us. But feels much more expansive and complicated than just, did we make something people want? Do they pay enough for it? Are they pulling it from us? That feels like there's a danger in thinking in that somewhat more narrow way that maybe not everybody thinks. But if I ask you to get to the moon, and you show me that you're a foot closer to the moon every day, not interesting. There's probably a ladder to the moon and I worry that there's a bunch of Product Market Fit that is so siloed. It's just building a ladder to the moon. You might build a pretty tall ladder, but you're not going to get to the moon that way.
zh: 我觉得有些人把Product Market Fit理解为，有人在为它付钱吗？那是一个超低的门槛。是正确类型的人在为它付钱吗？那是一个稍高的门槛。他们为它付的钱比我为造出这东西的成本更多吗？那是一个稍高的门槛。我找到这些人并说服他们购买的代价有多高，而不是他们来找我发现我？我们在从艰难推送到轻松拉力的光谱上处于什么位置？这些事情很重要，但如果你在努力活到再战一天。也许那一篮子东西基本就是全部了。产品层面还有一些别的东西，比如当你不在场时，一个分销商向别人解释这东西有多容易？在一个真正成品的产品里这相当重要。但在X，我们更关注的是像这样的事情：这个行业的穴位在哪里？或者，比如，我们对电网有一个登月计划。但你无法在实验室里造一个假的小电网并从中学到任何东西。而且你不能一开始就去找这些电网运营商说，把你们所有的数据给我，我要为你们做一个小东西。这对世界上每个国家来说都是国家安全层面的事。他们就是不会做的。我们花了五年时间做那些能帮助我们深入理解他们问题的事情。这样我们才能开始帮助他们，而我们做的最初几件事甚至不是那个登月计划。只是建立起融洽关系，这样我们才能和世界上的电网运营商一起，开始把他们的电网运营、规划和优化带进21世纪。但我们投入了五六年的工作，那些工作不是以产品为焦点，只是看起来有点像以产品为焦点，但它不是Product Market Fit。因为那不是我们真正在做的，我们其实是在试图与合作伙伴契合，这样我们才能和他们进入一种节奏。这样我们才能再去构建能解决他们问题的东西。这就是对我们来说感觉像moonshot market fit的一个例子。但它感觉比“我们做了人们想要的东西吗？他们为它付了足够的钱吗？他们在从我们这里拉走它吗？”这种思路要宽广和复杂得多。以那种稍微更狭窄的方式思考存在危险，虽然可能不是每个人都这么想。但如果我让你去月球，而你向我展示你每天都离月球近一英尺，没意思。大概有一架通往月球的梯子，而我担心有很多Product Market Fit是如此孤岛化。那就是在造一架通往月球的梯子。你也许能造一架相当高的梯子，但你不会以那种方式到达月球。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: So does that come down to finding the biggest part of the problem or something? I'm trying to maybe get more granularity on that. Is that how you think about it?
zh: 所以这归结为找到问题最大的部分或类似的东西吗？我试图也许在这方面得到更多细节。你是这样考虑的吗？

speaker: Astro Teller
en: Sometimes it's the biggest part of the problem. Sometimes it's like, if you want to change a system fundamentally, then finding how to sell to the incumbents is very complicated. Because if you sell to the incumbents and they don't want the system to change. That's an example where you end up potentially depending on the incumbents, building a ladder to the moon. Because they will give you money. You can make a medium sized business. You can make a billion dollars a year selling to incumbents. But you're probably not going to change some huge industry if the incumbents, who are your main customers, don't want the industry to change. That's the kind of tension that we feel like we're holding here a lot. It's like, what would really change the industry? And then work backwards from there. Who are we going to have to work with first? Sometimes it could be the incumbents, but then we need to start with, we're going to blow up your industry. Are you interested in doing that with us? If not, please do not sign up with us. You'll just be angry at us later and we say that to people, and many of them tell us to pound sand. But that's a little bit like the monkey also. If that's where the problem is, let's be honest about it.
zh: 有时是问题最大的部分。有时是像这样：如果你想从根本上改变一个系统，那么找到如何卖给在位者的方法就非常复杂。因为如果你卖给在位者，而他们不希望系统改变。那就是一个例子，你最终可能依赖于在位者，造一架通往月球的梯子。因为他们会给你钱。你可以做成一个中等规模的生意。你可以通过卖给在位者一年赚十亿美元。但如果那些作为你主要客户的在位者不希望这个行业改变，你大概率不会改变某个巨大的行业。那种张力就是我们在很大程度上经常感受到的。就是，什么才会真正改变这个行业？然后从那里往回推。我们首先得和谁合作？有时可能是在位者，但那时我们需要从这一点开始：我们要炸掉你们的行业。你有兴趣和我们一起做吗？如果没有，请不要与我们签约。你以后只会对我们生气，我们对人们就是这么说的，而他们中很多人让我们滚开。但这也有点像那只猴子。如果问题就在那里，那就诚实地面对它。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Perfect, well, listen, I think that's a perfect place to stop. I'll ask maybe just one more question. What would be a top piece of advice that you would have for early stage founders that are in their pre Product Market Fit? Maybe they have an idea, maybe they don't yet. Maybe they've got signals of something kind of working. What would you say to them, having built and worked with so many ideas over the last decade plus?
zh: 完美，好吧，听着，我觉得那是一个完美的收尾点。我也许再问最后一个问题。对于处于Product Market Fit之前的早期创始人，你最重要的建议是什么？也许他们有一个想法，也许还没有。也许他们有了某些东西在起作用的信号。在过去十年多的时间里构建并合作过这么多想法之后，你会对他们说什么？

speaker: Astro Teller
en: I'm going to give you a very non traditional answer, but I deeply believe it. The hardest and most important thing for anyone to learn is, some people would call it managing their own psychology. Some people would call it wisdom, personal growth, but the extent to which people don't really understand themselves and their relationship to the world. Where there are inner forces that are driving them in pretty complex ways. Causes them to be so imperfect as managers and leaders. I guarantee you, for most of your listeners, doing that hard personal inner work will pay more dividends over the next ten years. Maybe your company will die in the meantime, I don't know. But over the next ten years, that's the thing that will supercharge them the most. Not hiring a better business development person.
zh: 我要给你一个非常非传统的答案，但我深信不疑。对任何人来说最难也最重要的学习是，有些人会称之为管理好自己的心理。有些人会称之为智慧、个人成长，但人们在多大程度上没有真正理解自己和与世界的关系。那里有一些内在力量以相当复杂的方式驱动着他们。这导致他们作为管理者和领导者如此不完美。我向你保证，对于你的大多数听众来说，做那种艰难的个人内在功课，在未来十年会带来更多回报。也许你的公司会在此期间死掉，我不知道。但在未来十年，那是最能给她们赋能的事情。不是雇一个更好的业务拓展人员。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Perfect, Astro, thanks so much for spending the time. It's been great.
zh: 完美，Astro，非常感谢你抽出时间。非常愉快。

speaker: Astro Teller
en: Thank you.
zh: 谢谢。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: So picture this. It's months from now, years from now and one of your founder friends. A really close founder friend of yours, guess what? Their startup went bankrupt and it turns out, if you had just shared the Product Market Fit Show with them. They would have learned everything they needed to find Product Market Fit and to create a huge success. But instead, their startup has completely failed. You have blood on your hands.
